clue.text: That's a very good thing, upon my word !

definitions.meaning: a holy thing or relic, something sacred one might swear by
the old oath 'by my ...' was an exclamation like 'upon my word'

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims with approval at something excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very good' stands for holy (the old sense of a holy relic or sanctuary), and the word was used in the archaic oath 'by my halidom'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a sacred relic or holy place, and it survives in an archaic oath equivalent to swearing on one's honour.

clue.text: He's terribly rash about love, is 5's accomplice

indicators.note: about says the rearranged letters go round the love
terribly signals that rash is scrambled

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: A man described as dreadfully hasty in love turns out to be a partner in crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' rearranges RASH to HRSA, and 'about' puts it round O. 5 is 5-across: Horsa was Hengist's brother and fellow Jute leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend makes him the brother and fellow commander of the Jute leader at 5-across.

clue.text: This man's a marginal landlubber !

parts.note: a dock worker spends his life at the water's edge, on the margin of the land but never at sea

explanation.surface: A man who barely counts as a land-dweller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marginal' points to the shore, the margin of the land; with 'man' added, the answer names a docker.
explanation.definitionFit: A docker works along the coast, at the margin of the sea, without sailing.

clue.text: Gadfly's victim in stage presentation of pictures.

indicators.note: in puts the victim inside the stage

parts.note: the stage stands for drama, theatre
in Greek myth Hera sent a gadfly to torment Io

explanation.surface: Someone bitten by a gadfly appears in a staged picture show.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Hera sent a gadfly to torment Io, so IO goes into DRAMA.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a scenic display of painted views or models, a show built around pictures.

clue.text: Two generations of in-laws for Mr. Rochester

parts.note: a mother, ma, is one generation
a son is the next generation down

explanation.surface: Asks what two generations of relatives by marriage the Jane Eyre hero had.
explanation.walkthrough: In Jane Eyre, Rochester's first wife was Bertha Mason, so her family were his in-laws.
explanation.definitionFit: Rochester married Bertha of this family in Jane Eyre, making her relatives his in-laws.

clue.text: The bird gets the message from the Jute leader

parts.note: a hen is a female bird
the gist is the essential message of something

explanation.surface: A bird picks up a communication from a tribal chief.
explanation.walkthrough: Hengist and his brother Horsa are the legendary leaders of the Jutes who settled in Kent in the fifth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend names this warrior as the chief who led the Jutish invaders of Britain.

clue.text: Where old Dobbin got his oats !

definitions.text: Where old Dobbin got his oats

parts.words: Where old Dobbin got his oats
parts.note: the word comes from an old term for a bag of oats for a horse; Dobbin is a stock name for a farm horse

explanation.surface: A question about where an old horse was fed.
explanation.walkthrough: Dobbin is a traditional British name for a farm horse; the bag's name comes from German Haber, oats, so it was first a horse's feed bag.
explanation.definitionFit: This shoulder bag was originally a cavalry bag holding oats for a horse.

clue.text: Now, hands together in front of the face

definitions.text: Now, hands together in front of the face

parts.words: Now, hands together in front of the face
parts.note: the clock's hands meet upright on its face at midday, as hands meet in prayer

explanation.surface: A command to put one's palms together in front of the face, as in prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: The hands and face are a clock's, not a person's: both hands point straight up together at midday.
explanation.definitionFit: At twelve o'clock in the day both hands of a clock coincide.

clue.text: I distribute only the best

parts.note: to deal is to distribute, as with cards

explanation.surface: Someone boasts they hand out nothing but the finest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something perfect is a model of excellence, nothing less than the finest.

clue.text: The lady's willing !

parts.note: 'willing' read as making a will: a woman who leaves a will

explanation.surface: A woman agreeing to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Willing' seems to mean eager, but it means drawing up a will; the answer is the feminine form for one who does.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the old feminine term for a woman who has made a will.

clue.text: It's right about Samson having huge sums

indicators.note: about here signals that the name Samson is turned around into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A remark that the strongman of the Bible had enormous wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning' in the surface but is the anagram signal working on the strongman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A king's ransom is proverbially a vast amount of money, so the plural stands for very large payments.

clue.text: dim, But sweeter than the lids of Juno's eyes " (W. Tale)

definitions.text: dim, But sweeter than the lids of Juno's eyes

parts.words: dim, But sweeter than the lids of Juno's eyes
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Perdita's flower speech in The Winter's Tale names the missing purple spring blooms

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale with its first word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank is filled from Perdita's lines in Act IV of The Winter's Tale: '___ dim, But sweeter than the lids of Juno's eyes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Perdita describes these small purple spring flowers as dim yet sweeter than the goddess's eyelids.

clue.text: Colourful composer among seamen, a dry lot !

indicators.note: among says one piece sits in the middle of the seamen

parts.note: ABs are able seamen, ordinary sailors
Sir John Stainer was an English composer, and a stainer is one who colours things

explanation.surface: A vividly dressed musician mixes with sailors, who turn out to be teetotal.
explanation.walkthrough: Sailors are proverbially heavy drinkers, so the dry crowd among them is a surprise; 'Colourful' is there because a stainer adds colour.
explanation.definitionFit: People who refuse alcohol are called dry, and a group of teetotallers is a dry lot.

clue.text: Every Scot has a leaning towards kail

indicators.note: a leaning tilts the letters of kail out of line into a new order

explanation.surface: A Scotsman is said to be fond of kale, the curly cabbage.
explanation.walkthrough: Kail is the Scots spelling of kale; 'has a leaning towards' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots dialect this word is the equivalent of 'each' or 'every'.

clue.text: Take a turn in the past

parts.note: a go is a turn in a game

explanation.surface: An instruction to have a turn at something, set in times gone by.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happened some time back happened earlier, in time already gone.

clue.text: Divine music in an Italian public library

definitions.meaning: the chant associated with St Ambrose, and also meaning heavenly, like the food of the gods
the famous library in Milan named after St Ambrose

explanation.surface: Heavenly music is to be heard in a library in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Ambrosian chant is the Milanese plainsong named after St Ambrose, and the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan was one of the first public libraries.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective names both the plainsong of St Ambrose, heavenly in sound, and the Milan library founded in his name.

clue.text: Just like the little beast !

parts.note: describes resemblance to a tiny creature, the microscopic organisms once called little animals

explanation.surface: An exclamation that someone is behaving exactly like a little monster.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a naughty child, but the 'little beast' is a microscopic creature, and the adjective describes something resembling one.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the tiny microscopic organisms once named little animals, so anything resembling one fits.

clue.text: "Grieving, if aught e'er grieves, Over the unreturning brave, alas !" (Byron)

definitions.text: Grieving, if aught e'er grieves, Over the unreturning brave, alas

parts.words: Grieving, if aught e'er grieves, Over the unreturning brave, alas
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Byron's Waterloo stanzas in Childe Harold, where the forest weeps for the dead

explanation.surface: A mournful line from Byron's poem on Waterloo with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron, Childe Harold III: the Ardennes leaves weep dew, 'Grieving, if aught ___ e'er grieves'; the gap is a word for lifeless things.
explanation.definitionFit: The forest is without life, so its grief is that of a lifeless thing.

clue.text: 'Shred' the garlic and you'll feel sleepy

indicators.note: shredding cuts the words the garlic to pieces, to be rebuilt in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Cooking advice warns that chopped garlic will make you drowsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shred' rearranges THE GARLIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling sluggish and drowsy is the state described by this adjective.

clue.text: Shopping equipment for little Mary

definitions.meaning: a basket for carrying loaves when shopping
a dated British euphemism for the stomach, from J. M. Barrie's play Little Mary

explanation.surface: Someone buys a shopping basket for a small girl named Mary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Mary' was a dated British nickname for the stomach, from J. M. Barrie's play; the answer is also slang for the belly.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a basket for loaves and old slang for the belly, where food ends up.

clue.text: Disciplined result of mild rebuke over nothing to a leftist

parts.note: tut is the sound made in mild reproof
O is zero, nothing
a red is a left-winger

explanation.surface: A socialist receives a gentle telling-off about having nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' is a down-clue link: each piece sits above the next; 'to a' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone schooled or trained has been taught under instruction, which is a form of discipline.

clue.text: Chancellor's cart ?

parts.note: the Chancellor of the Exchequer levies duties

explanation.surface: A question about what vehicle the Chancellor drives.
explanation.walkthrough: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is the UK finance minister; a tax-cart was a light cart on which a low duty was paid, so the word pairs with cart.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chancellor's business is levying duties, and those duties also named a light farm cart.

clue.text: Bad language might be by my 1 across

definitions.text: Bad language might be by my 1 across

parts.words: Bad language might be by my 1 across
parts.note: the archaic exclamation 'by my' followed by the 1-across answer is a form of swearing

explanation.surface: Someone warns that coarse speech might follow an old exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad language' suggests rudeness, but here it means swearing in the old sense: the phrase 'by my' plus the 1-across word is a sworn exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Swearing by something sacred is a solemn declaration, also a word for a curse or profanity.

clue.text: With which to grab the cards ?

definitions.meaning: a claw, which a bird of prey grips with
the stock of cards left over after the deal in some card games

explanation.surface: A question about what to use to snatch the playing cards.
explanation.walkthrough: In card games such as patience, the cards left after the deal are also called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a bird of prey's claw, used for seizing, and the stock left after dealing.

clue.text: Smallest saint is given to bombast when on duty

parts.note: read as mini plus st, the clue's 'Smallest' supplies mini, meaning small
rant is bombastic, ranting speech

explanation.surface: A tiny saint is said to be prone to pompous speech while working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smallest' is read as two parts, small plus the saint's abbreviation; a ministrant is one who serves at an altar.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes one who ministers or attends, serving at an altar while carrying out duties.

clue.text: Such notions can be put aside

indicators.note: can be put signals the letters of aside are placed in another order

explanation.surface: Some thoughts may be set aside for later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be put' rearranges ASIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Notions and thoughts are synonyms, plans or concepts held in the mind.

clue.text: "Now the salt — seaward flow" (Arnold)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Matthew Arnold's The Forsaken Merman, naming the sea's ebb and flow

explanation.surface: A line from Matthew Arnold's poem about the sea with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Arnold's The Forsaken Merman: 'Now the salt ___ seaward flow'; the missing word is the sea's rising and falling.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea's regular rise and fall are what flow seaward on the ebb.

clue.text: This old dame might be wrong

indicators.note: might be suggests the word could become something else by rearrangement

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: An elderly woman might be in the wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' rearranges TORT, the legal word for a civil wrong; an old trot is a dated term for an old woman.
explanation.definitionFit: This dated word for an old woman, usually unkind, is found in Shakespeare.

clue.text: " And what should I do in -" (T. Night)

definitions.text: And what should I do in

parts.words: And what should I do in
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Viola's question on landing in Twelfth Night ends with the country she has been shipwrecked in

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Twelfth Night with its last word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Viola, washed ashore in Act I of Twelfth Night, asks: 'And what should I do in ___?'
explanation.definitionFit: The shipwrecked heroine of the comedy lands in this ancient Adriatic country, the play's setting.

clue.text: Angered? Let's put it this way

definitions.text: Angered? Let's put it this way

indicators.note: the phrase invites rewording, and here the letters of Angered are put a different way into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone cross is asked whether they are cross, and offered another way of saying it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let's put it this way' rearranges ANGERED, and the result says the same thing in other words.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean made furious, so the rearrangement is a synonym of the word it comes from.

clue.text: She's restricted by a double negative

definitions.text: She's restricted by a double negative

parts.words: She's restricted by a double negative
parts.note: the 1925 musical title puts two refusals in front of this girl's name

explanation.surface: A woman is held back by a pair of refusals.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'double negative' is the two refusals in the title of the musical No, No, ___, which sit in front of the girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the girl's name in the musical title preceded by two refusals.

clue.text: French nobleman in ecclesiastical offices corrupts!

indicators.note: in places the nobleman inside the bishops' offices

parts.note: a see is a bishop's office or diocese
duc is French for duke

explanation.surface: A French aristocrat in the bishop's palace leads people astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offices' suggests workplaces, but a see is a bishop's seat; 'in' puts the French duke inside two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: To lead someone astray morally is to corrupt them, often by tempting them.
